record.title: OSWorld-Pro adds process-level diagnostics to computer-use evaluation
record.summary: The September 2026 OSWorld-Pro preprint introduces a process-based benchmark for computer-use agents with more than 300 tasks, 2,800 sequential subgoals and over 67,000 human annotations. Authors use human-aligned language-model judges to score subgoal fulfillment through trajectories. They report Claude Opus 5 at 75.7% on OSWorld-Pro versus 83.4% on OSWorld and identify failure patterns such as irrelevant actions and click mistakes.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Authors report a benchmark of 300+ tasks, 2,800+ subgoals and 67,000+ human annotations. Their reported top score for Claude Opus 5 is 75.7% on OSWorld-Pro versus 83.4% on OSWorld; they identify subgoal-irrelevant actions and click-based mistakes as process-level failure modes.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv record identifies the paper and its submission/revision metadata. This confirms that the preprint was posted, not that its experimental claims have been independently established.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or blind, failure-class-specific human audit of the LLM judges was inspected.
No test of whether process scores predict future task success or improve interventions was inspected.

brief.importance_rationale: If its process labels and judges remain reliable across varied tasks, the benchmark could change how teams diagnose and target computer-use agent failures. It is an evaluation contribution rather than a capability result, and judge validity and valid alternative paths remain important constraints.
limitations: Quantitative results and judge quality are author-reported; no independent reproduction or blind audit was inspected.
The 75.7% OSWorld-Pro and 83.4% OSWorld figures are from different task/evaluation regimes and are not directly interpretable as an absolute hidden-error estimate.
Process annotations may privilege a preferred path and miss valid alternative trajectories; rare GUI states may remain underrepresented.
Language-model judging adds model dependence and evaluation cost; agreement by failure type and operational usefulness are not established here.

Authors use human-aligned language-model judges to score subgoal fulfillment through trajectories. They report Claude Opus 5 at 75.7% on OSWorld-Pro versus 83.4% on OSWorld and identify failure patterns such as irrelevant actions and click mistakes.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report a benchmark of 300+ tasks, 2,800+ subgoals and 67,000+ human annotations. Their reported top score for Claude Opus 5 is 75.7% on OSWorld-Pro versus 83.4% on OSWorld; they identify subgoal-irrelevant actions and click-based mistakes as process-level failure modes.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv preprint and its method/experimental design were inspected. The numerical outcome is reported by the paper authors and is not independently demonstrated in this review.
technical.mechanism: The benchmark decomposes long desktop tasks into sequential subgoals grounded in human annotations and applies language-model judges to estimate whether each subgoal is fulfilled as the trajectory unfolds.
technical.regime: Author-run benchmark evaluation of computer-use agents on sequential desktop tasks with human annotations and language-model judges; reported OSWorld score comparison uses the paper’s benchmark configurations.
technical.strongest_baseline: OSWorld end-state functional evaluation; reported Claude Opus 5 scores are 75.7% on OSWorld-Pro and 83.4% on OSWorld. Difference should not be read as a hidden error-rate estimate because task sets and evaluation regimes differ.

brief.title: OSWorld-Pro adds process-level diagnostics to computer-use evaluation
brief.why_it_matters: A final artifact score hides where a long computer-use trajectory failed. Process-level labels may distinguish subgoal selection, action execution and recovery errors, making interventions more targeted; they also introduce annotation and judge-model costs and can mis-score valid alternative paths.
